message.content:
Below is a concise, practical guide to the key rights you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | # | Right | What it means for you | Practical Tips | |---|-------|-----------------------|----------------| | **1** | **Right to a written lease (if you sign one)** | Texas law requires a written lease if the tenancy lasts longer than 30 days. The lease must state the rent amount, due date, security‑deposit amount, and the length of the tenancy. | Keep a copy of the lease (paper or electronic). If you only signed a verbal agreement, you still have the same rights, but a written lease makes enforcement easier. | | **2** | **Right to a safe, habitable home** | The landlord must keep the premises in a condition that meets basic health and safety standards (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, no mold, no pest infestation). | Document any problems (photos, dates, emails). Notify the landlord in writing and give a reasonable time to fix the issue. | | **3** | **Right to privacy** | Landlords may enter the premises only for:
• Emergency repairs
• Inspections after giving at least 24 hours’ notice (or 48 hours for non‑emergencies)
• To show the unit to prospective buyers/renters (after 24 hours’ notice) | Keep a log of all entries. If a landlord enters without proper notice, you can refuse entry. | | **4** | **Right to a security deposit limit** | Texas limits the security deposit to **no more than one month’s rent** for a month‑to‑month tenancy. For a fixed‑term lease, the deposit can be up to **two months’ rent**. | Ask for a written receipt. The landlord must return the deposit within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | | **5** | **Right to receive a written itemized list of deductions** | If the landlord keeps any portion of your deposit, they must provide a written, itemized statement within 30 days of the move‑out date. | Review the statement carefully. If you disagree, you can dispute it in small‑claims court. | | **6** | **Right to a fair eviction process** | Evictions must follow Texas Property Code § 24.005–24.015. The landlord must:
• Serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination, 60‑day notice for rent increase).
• File a lawsuit if you do not comply. | Keep copies of all notices. If you receive a notice, respond promptly (pay the rent, negotiate, or move out). | | **7** | **Right to challenge unlawful rent increases** | Rent increases must be in writing and cannot exceed the amount specified in the lease. For month‑to‑month tenants, the landlord can raise rent with a 30‑day notice. | Verify the notice meets the legal requirements. If it doesn’t, you may refuse to pay the increase. | | **8** | **Right to be free from discrimination** | Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **9** | **Right to a written lease amendment** | Any changes to the lease (rent, utilities, pet policy, etc.) must be documented in writing and signed by both parties. | Request a written amendment if the landlord verbally promises a change. | | **10** | **Right to a refund of over‑paid rent** | If you pay more than the agreed rent (e.g., due to a mistake), the landlord must refund the excess. | Keep records of all payments. If the landlord refuses, you can seek a refund through the court. | --- ### Quick Reference Checklist 1. **Lease** – Verify it’s in writing and includes rent, deposit, term, and contact info. 2. **Security Deposit** – Confirm it does not exceed the statutory limit. 3. **Notice Requirements** – Know the required notice periods for rent increases, lease termination, and entry. 4. **Habitability** – Document any maintenance issues and give the landlord written notice. 5. **Eviction Process** – Understand the types of notices and the timeline for legal action. 6. **Discrimination** – Know your rights under state and federal fair‑housing laws. --- ### Resources | Resource | What it offers | How to access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Fair‑housing complaints | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Federal fair‑housing enforcement | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Texas Tenant Rights Hotline** | Phone support (if available) | Check local tenant‑rights groups or legal aid websites | | **Legal Aid of North Texas** | Free legal assistance | https://www.lanxt.org/ | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Process for disputes over deposits, rent, etc. | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful eviction notice** (e.g., no proper notice, or the landlord entered without permission). - **Discrimination claim** (e.g., being denied a lease or facing harassment). - **Security deposit disputes** (e.g., landlord keeps deposit without valid reason). - **Habitability violations** that the landlord refuses to fix. If you’re unsure about any situation, it’s often worth calling a local tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a written lease, a safe and habitable home, privacy, a limited security deposit, a fair eviction process, and protection against discrimination. Keep thorough records, communicate in writing, and know the statutory notice requirements to protect yourself.
